summary: Saul is in hearty agreement with Stephen's execution, linking the end of the Stephen narrative to the beginning of the persecution that follows.

section_title: The Great Persecution and the Scattering
summary: A great persecution begins against the Jerusalem church; all except the apostles are scattered throughout Judea and Samaria; devout men bury Stephen with loud lamentation; Saul begins ravaging the church, dragging off men and women to prison.

section_title: The Scattered Ones Preach the Word
summary: Those who have been scattered go about preaching the word, transforming persecution into mission expansion.

section_title: Philip in Samaria
summary: Philip goes down to the city of Samaria and proclaims the Christ; the crowds pay attention with one accord, unclean spirits come out, the paralyzed and lame are healed, and there is much rejoicing in that city.

section_title: Simon the Magician
summary: Simon, who had previously practiced magic and amazed the people of Samaria claiming to be someone great, sees Philip's signs and message; Simon himself believes and is baptized, and continues on with Philip, constantly amazed at the signs and great miracles being performed.

section_title: The Apostles Send Peter and John
summary: The apostles in Jerusalem send Peter and John to Samaria; they pray for the new believers to receive the Holy Spirit, since the Spirit had not yet fallen on any of them -- they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus; then Peter and John lay hands on them and they receive the Holy Spirit.

section_title: Simon's Attempt to Purchase the Spirit's Power
summary: Simon sees that the Spirit is given through the laying on of the apostles' hands and offers them money, asking for the same authority; Peter responds with a devastating rebuke: Simon's silver should perish with him for thinking God's gift could be purchased; he has no part or share in this matter because his heart is not right before God; he is in the gall of bitterness and bondage of unrighteousness; he must repent and pray to the Lord if possible for forgiveness.
relevance: This passage is critical to the permanence-versus-conditionality question. Simon is explicitly described as having 'believed' and 'been baptized' (8:13) -- the same verbs used for genuine converts throughout Acts. Yet Peter tells him he has 'no part or share in this matter' (8:21), his 'heart is not right before God' (8:21), he is in the 'gall of bitterness and bondage of unrighteousness' (8:23), and his forgiveness is conditional: 'if possible (ei ara), the intention of your heart will be forgiven you' (8:22). The neutral reading explicitly states: 'Luke does not say Simon's belief was fake -- he uses the same vocabulary he uses everywhere else for genuine response to the gospel. The problem is not that Simon never believed but that his heart is not right before God.' The neutral reading further draws the principle: 'believing and being baptized is the beginning of the journey, not its automatic completion.' Whether Simon represents failed initial belief or genuine belief that went wrong, the passage establishes that belief-plus-baptism does not automatically guarantee a right standing before God, and that forgiveness after failure within the community is conditional rather than guaranteed.
key_phrases: May your silver perish with you
you have no part or share in this matter
your heart is not right before God
you are in the gall of bitterness and bondage of unrighteousness
if possible, the intention of your heart will be forgiven you

section_title: Return to Jerusalem
summary: Peter and John return to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel to many villages of the Samaritans along the way.

section_title: Philip Directed to the Desert Road
summary: An angel of the Lord directs Philip to go south on the desert road from Jerusalem to Gaza; there he encounters an Ethiopian eunuch, a court official of the Candace, who has come to Jerusalem to worship and is reading from Isaiah; the Spirit tells Philip to go up and join the chariot.

section_title: Philip Interprets Isaiah for the Ethiopian
summary: Philip hears the eunuch reading Isaiah 53 and asks if he understands it; the eunuch invites Philip to guide him; Philip begins from that Scripture and proclaims Jesus to him.

section_title: The Ethiopian Eunuch's Baptism
summary: The eunuch sees water and asks what prevents him from being baptized; they go down into the water and Philip baptizes him; the Spirit of the Lord snatches Philip away, and the eunuch goes on his way rejoicing.

section_title: Philip's Continuing Mission
summary: Philip is found at Azotus and keeps preaching the gospel to all the cities until he comes to Caesarea.

section_title: Saul's Mission of Persecution
summary: Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the Lord's disciples, obtains letters from the high priest to the synagogues at Damascus to bring any who belong to the Way, both men and women, bound to Jerusalem.

section_title: The Encounter on the Road to Damascus
summary: A light from heaven flashes around Saul; he falls to the ground and hears the voice of Jesus asking 'Why are you persecuting Me?'; Saul is blinded for three days, during which he neither eats nor drinks.

section_title: The Vision to Ananias and the Commission of Saul
summary: The Lord appears to Ananias in a vision and sends him to Saul, calling Saul a 'chosen instrument' (skeuos ekloges) to bear God's name before Gentiles, kings, and the sons of Israel, and declaring that Saul will be shown how much he must suffer for Jesus's name. The 'chosen instrument' language describes vocational calling -- election to a specific mission and purpose -- not a guarantee of individual eternal salvation.

section_title: Ananias's Obedience and Saul's Healing
summary: Ananias goes to Saul, lays hands on him, addresses him as 'Brother Saul,' declares that the Lord Jesus who appeared to him on the road has sent him so that Saul may regain his sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit; something like scales falls from Saul's eyes and he is baptized.

section_title: Saul Preaching in Damascus
summary: Saul spends several days with the disciples in Damascus and immediately begins proclaiming Jesus in the synagogues, declaring that Jesus is the Son of God; all who hear are amazed; Saul keeps increasing in strength and confounding the Jews by proving that Jesus is the Christ.

section_title: The Plot Against Saul and His Escape
summary: After many days the Jews plot together to kill Saul; their plot becomes known; the disciples lower him in a basket through an opening in the city wall by night.

section_title: Saul in Jerusalem
summary: Saul comes to Jerusalem and tries to associate with the disciples, but they are all afraid of him; Barnabas brings him to the apostles and describes his conversion and bold preaching; Saul speaks boldly in Jesus's name, disputes with the Hellenistic Jews, and when the brethren learn of a plot against his life, they send him to Tarsus.

section_title: The Peace Summary
summary: The church throughout Judea, Galilee, and Samaria enjoys peace, is built up, and continues to increase, walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit.

section_title: Peter Heals Aeneas at Lydda
summary: Peter travels to Lydda, finds a paralyzed man named Aeneas who has been bedridden for eight years, heals him in the name of Jesus Christ, and all who live at Lydda and Sharon see him and turn to the Lord.

section_title: Peter Raises Tabitha at Joppa
summary: In Joppa, a disciple named Tabitha (Dorcas) who was full of good works and charity falls sick and dies; Peter is summoned, prays, and raises her from the dead; the miracle becomes known throughout Joppa and many believe in the Lord.

section_title: Cornelius -- A Gentile Described in Israel's Vocabulary
summary: The neutral reading identifies Cornelius as a Roman centurion and God-fearer who feared God, gave alms to the Jewish people, and prayed continually -- a Gentile who had done everything possible to approach Israel's God without becoming an Israelite.

section_title: The Angel's Instruction to Cornelius
summary: An angel tells Cornelius at the hour of sacrifice that his prayers and alms have ascended as a memorial offering before God, and directs him to send for Peter in Joppa.

section_title: Peter's Vision -- The Sheet from Heaven
summary: Peter receives a thrice-repeated vision of a sheet containing clean and unclean animals together, with the divine command 'What God has made clean, do not call common' -- a dismantling of the dietary laws that embodied Israel's ethnic separation from the nations.

section_title: The Spirit Interprets the Vision
summary: While Peter is perplexed about the vision's meaning, the Spirit directs him to go with Cornelius's Gentile messengers 'without hesitation' (meden diakrinomenos -- making no distinction), claiming ownership of their mission: 'I have sent them.'

section_title: Peter Enters a Gentile's House
summary: Peter enters Cornelius's house with Jewish witnesses and states the interpretation of his vision: 'God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean' -- the food laws were about people, and the ethnic boundary they enforced has been dissolved by divine action.

section_title: Cornelius Recounts His Vision
summary: Cornelius retells his angelic visitation and declares that the entire household is assembled 'in the presence of God to hear all that you have been commanded by the Lord.'

section_title: Peter's Speech -- God Shows No Partiality
summary: Peter declares that God shows no partiality and that in every nation anyone who fears God and does what is right is acceptable to him, then proclaims the gospel of Jesus's life, death, resurrection, and appointment as judge, concluding that 'everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.'

section_title: The Spirit Falls on the Gentiles
summary: While Peter is still speaking, the Holy Spirit falls on all who hear the word -- unilaterally, without apostolic laying on of hands, without baptism, without circumcision -- producing the same phenomena as Pentecost (tongues, praise of God).
relevance: The Spirit's action is entirely sovereign and unilateral: God gives the gift without human mediation, precondition, or qualification. The neutral reading emphasizes that 'God acted first, preempting every human gatekeeping mechanism' and that the Spirit 'acts unilaterally.' This pattern of divine initiative -- God granting the gift apart from human qualification or cooperation -- could be read as supporting the permanence of what God unilaterally bestows. However, the text is primarily about who can receive the gift (Gentiles as well as Jews), not about whether the gift, once received, is irrevocable.
key_phrases: the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word
the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles
the Spirit acts unilaterally

section_title: Baptism -- The Human Response to God's Action
summary: Peter declares that no one can withhold baptism from those who have received the Holy Spirit 'just as we have,' commands their baptism in Jesus's name, and stays with the Gentile household for some days in table fellowship.

section_title: Jerusalem's Acceptance of Gentile Inclusion
summary: Peter defends his table fellowship with Gentiles by retelling the Cornelius episode, concluding 'If then God gave the same gift to them as he gave to us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could stand in God's way?'; the Jerusalem community responds by acknowledging 'Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life.'
relevance: The phrase 'God has granted repentance that leads to life' (v. 18) uses gift language (edoken) for repentance and life -- both are presented as divine grants, not human achievements. Peter's argument rests on God's sovereign initiative: God gave the Spirit without human precondition, and Peter could not 'stand in God's way.' This framing of salvation as God's unilateral gift has implications for permanence, since what God grants by sovereign initiative may not be contingent on human performance. However, the neutral reading explicitly notes a tension with 11:23, and the passage is primarily about the fact of Gentile inclusion rather than about whether that inclusion is irrevocable.
key_phrases: God gave the same gift to them as he gave to us
who was I that I could stand in God's way
God has granted repentance that leads to life

section_title: The Antioch Community -- Expansion and Exhortation
summary: The scattering after Stephen's death produces a mixed community at Antioch where Gentiles believe in large numbers; Barnabas is sent from Jerusalem and upon arrival 'exhorted them all to remain true to the Lord with resolute heart' (prosmenein te kardia te kyrio).
relevance: The neutral reading identifies a deliberate tension between the gift language of v. 18 ('God has granted repentance that leads to life') and the exhortation language of v. 23 ('remain true to the Lord with resolute heart'). The verb prosmenein ('to remain in, to continue with, to stay faithful to') presupposes that remaining is not automatic -- if it were guaranteed, the exhortation would be pointless. The neutral reading connects this to Deuteronomy 30 and Ezekiel 18 covenant dynamics where life is contingent on ongoing faithfulness. The tension is significant: God grants repentance that leads to life, AND believers must be exhorted to remain in what God has granted.
key_phrases: exhorted them all to remain true to the Lord with resolute heart
prosmenein
the exhortation presupposes that remaining is not automatic

section_title: The Famine Relief Collection
summary: Agabus prophesies a famine, and the Antioch disciples send relief to the brothers in Judea through Barnabas and Saul -- an act of inter-community solidarity that demonstrates the practical outworking of the Gentile believers' faith.

section_title: Herod Kills James; Peter Imprisoned
summary: Herod Agrippa I kills the apostle James (brother of John) with the sword and arrests Peter during Passover, intending to execute him after the festival, while the church prays earnestly for Peter.

section_title: Peter's Miraculous Deliverance
summary: An angel rescues Peter from prison on the night before his scheduled execution -- chains fall off, gates open, and Peter is led past guards to freedom -- while the praying community initially cannot believe it when Peter arrives at their door.

section_title: Herod's Death and the Word's Growth
summary: Herod accepts divine acclamation ('the voice of a god, and not of a man'), is struck down by an angel of the Lord because he 'did not give God the glory,' and dies consumed by worms; the chapter closes with the summary 'the word of God increased and multiplied.'

section_title: The Spirit Commissions the First Deliberate Mission
summary: During worship and fasting at Antioch, the Holy Spirit commands the community to set apart Barnabas and Saul for the work to which he has already called them; the church lays hands on them and sends them off.

section_title: The Mission Begins in the Synagogues
summary: Sent out by the Holy Spirit, Barnabas and Saul sail to Cyprus and proclaim the word of God in the synagogues at Salamis, with John Mark assisting.

section_title: A Jewish False Prophet, a Gentile Proconsul, and the Name Paul
summary: At Paphos, the Jewish magician Bar-Jesus opposes the missionaries and tries to turn the proconsul Sergius Paulus from the faith; Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, pronounces temporary blindness on Bar-Jesus, and the proconsul believes.

section_title: Pisidian Antioch -- An Invitation to Speak
summary: Paul and companions travel to Pisidian Antioch, where they enter the synagogue on the Sabbath and are invited by the rulers to give a word of encouragement; John Mark departs and returns to Jerusalem.

section_title: Israel's History as God's Initiative
summary: Paul addresses the synagogue audience (both 'men of Israel' and God-fearers) with a historical review in which God is the subject of every verb: God chose the fathers, made the people great in Egypt, led them out, endured the wilderness, gave the land, provided judges, gave Saul as king, then raised up David as a man after God's own heart.

section_title: From David's Offspring to Jesus
summary: Paul declares that from David's offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as promised, with John the Baptist serving as the forerunner who pointed beyond himself to the one coming after him.

section_title: Jerusalem's Rejection as Prophetic Fulfillment
summary: Paul addresses both Jews and God-fearers as recipients of the salvation message, then declares that Jerusalem's rulers, by failing to recognize Jesus and condemning him, ironically fulfilled the very prophetic scriptures they read every Sabbath.

section_title: The Resurrection Proven from Scripture
summary: Paul argues that God raised Jesus from the dead, proving it from Psalm 2:7 (enthronement as God's Son), Isaiah 55:3 (the sure blessings of David requiring a living recipient), and Psalm 16:10 (God's Holy One will not see corruption) -- David himself died and decayed, so the psalm must refer to Jesus whom God raised.

section_title: Forgiveness Beyond the Law, and a Warning
summary: Paul declares that through Jesus forgiveness of sins is proclaimed and that 'everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses,' then warns with Habakkuk 1:5 that God is doing an unbelievable work and the hearers must not be among those who refuse to believe it.

section_title: The Initial Response -- Urged to Continue in Grace
summary: After the synagogue service, many Jews and devout proselytes follow Paul and Barnabas, who urge them 'to continue in the grace of God' (prosmenein te chariti tou theou).
relevance: The verb prosmenein ('to remain in, to continue in, to abide in') presupposes that remaining in God's grace is not automatic. The neutral reading notes that 'the exhortation to continue assumes that the response of faith is not a one-time event but an ongoing posture. Grace has been extended; they must remain in it.' This is the same verb (prosmenein) used in Acts 11:23, where Barnabas urges the Antioch believers to remain true to the Lord. The consistent use of this verb for exhorting believers to persist in what they have received implies that persistence is both necessary and not guaranteed.
key_phrases: urged them to continue in the grace of God
prosmenein te chariti tou theou

section_title: Jewish Jealousy and the Turn to the Gentiles
summary: When almost the whole city gathers the next Sabbath, the Jews are filled with jealousy and contradict Paul; Paul declares 'Since you thrust it aside and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we are turning to the Gentiles,' grounding this turn in Isaiah 49:6.
relevance: The phrase 'you judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life' uses active, reflexive verbs -- the rejection is self-determined, not divinely imposed. The neutral reading emphasizes the deliberate contrast: 'No one has judged them unworthy. God has not excluded them. They have excluded themselves.' While this describes the initial rejection of the gospel rather than a believer losing standing, it establishes the principle that human response determines one's relationship to eternal life. Eternal life is available, but human beings can exclude themselves from it by their own choices.
key_phrases: you thrust it aside
judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life
they have excluded themselves

section_title: The Response of the Gentiles -- Appointed to Eternal Life
summary: The Gentiles rejoice and glorify the word of the Lord, and 'as many as were appointed to eternal life believed' -- using the passive voice (tetagmenoi, from tasso) to describe their reception in contrast to the active verbs of Jewish self-exclusion.
relevance: The neutral reading identifies a 'deliberate asymmetry' between v. 46 (active, reflexive verbs for rejection) and v. 48 (passive verb for reception): 'rejection is described with active verbs (human choice), reception corresponds to a divine arrangement.' The passive participle tetagmenoi ('having been appointed/arranged/enrolled') indicates that the Gentiles' reception of eternal life corresponds to a prior divine ordering. If God has appointed people to eternal life, this could imply that what God has arranged is not contingent on fluctuating human performance. However, the neutral reading carefully notes that the author 'does not elaborate on the mechanism or timing of the appointment' and is narrating what happened rather than constructing a theory about the relationship between divine appointment and human response.
key_phrases: as many as were appointed to eternal life believed
tetagmenoi
passive voice indicating divine arrangement

section_title: The Word Spreads, Persecution Comes, Joy Remains
summary: The word of the Lord spreads throughout the region; the Jews incite persecution that drives Paul and Barnabas from the district; the new disciples left behind are filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.

section_title: Iconium -- The Pattern Repeats and Intensifies
summary: At Iconium, Paul and Barnabas speak in the synagogue and a large number of both Jews and Greeks believe; unbelieving Jews stir up opposition; the missionaries spend a long time there speaking boldly, with the Lord confirming the word of his grace through signs and wonders.

section_title: Division, Threat, and Flight to Lycaonia
summary: The city divides between those aligned with the Jews and those aligned with the apostles; when an attempt is made to stone them, Paul and Barnabas flee to Lystra and Derbe and continue preaching the gospel.

section_title: A Lame Man Healed at Lystra
summary: At Lystra, Paul heals a man crippled from birth who 'had faith to be made well,' commanding him to stand -- and the man immediately leaps up and walks.

section_title: The Crowd's Pagan Response -- Zeus and Hermes
summary: The pagan crowd misidentifies Barnabas and Paul as Zeus and Hermes and attempts to offer sacrifices to them -- a response that demonstrates the gap between the missionaries' message and the religious framework of their audience.

section_title: Paul's Speech to Pagans -- The Living God Who Made Everything
summary: Paul and Barnabas tear their garments, reject the worship, and redirect the crowd to 'a living God, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and all that is in them,' declaring that in past generations God allowed the nations to walk in their own ways while nevertheless providing rain, fruitful seasons, and food.

section_title: The Stoning of Paul
summary: Jews from Antioch and Iconium pursue the missionaries, persuade the crowds, stone Paul, and drag him out of the city supposing him dead; when the disciples gather around him, he rises and enters the city, departing the next day for Derbe.

section_title: The Return Journey -- Strengthening, Exhorting, Organizing
summary: After making disciples at Derbe, Paul and Barnabas retrace their route through hostile cities, 'strengthening the souls of the disciples, encouraging them to continue in the faith, and saying that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God'; they appoint elders in every church and entrust the communities to the Lord in whom they had believed.
relevance: The verb emmenein ('to remain in, to persevere in') demands ongoing commitment and presupposes that continuing is not automatic. The neutral reading states explicitly: 'If perseverance were guaranteed, the exhortation would be pointless. The fact that Paul urges these new believers to continue in the faith implies that not continuing is a real possibility -- that the pressures of tribulation could lead some to abandon what they have embraced.' Furthermore, the kingdom of God is presented as something to be 'entered' (eiselthein) through many tribulations -- a future destination reached by enduring, not a present possession that cannot be lost. The consistent pattern of exhortation verbs across Acts (prosmenein in 11:23 and 13:43, emmenein here in 14:22) creates a sustained argument that ongoing faithfulness is both necessary and non-guaranteed.
key_phrases: encouraging them to continue in the faith
emmenein te pistei
through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God
if perseverance were guaranteed, the exhortation would be pointless

section_title: The Return to Antioch -- Report to the Sending Church
summary: Paul and Barnabas return to Antioch in Syria and report to the sending church 'all the things that God had done with them and how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles,' then remain there for a long time.

section_title: The Crisis at Antioch
summary: Men from Judea teach at Antioch that circumcision according to the custom of Moses is necessary for salvation, provoking sharp dissension and debate with Paul and Barnabas, who are appointed to go to Jerusalem to resolve the question with the apostles and elders.

section_title: The Journey Through Phoenicia and Samaria
summary: En route to Jerusalem, Paul and Barnabas describe the conversion of the Gentiles in detail to the communities in Phoenicia and Samaria, bringing great joy to all the brothers.

section_title: Arrival in Jerusalem and the Pharisee Believers' Demand
summary: Paul and Barnabas are welcomed in Jerusalem and report what God has done; believers from the party of the Pharisees insist that Gentile believers must be circumcised and ordered to keep the law of Moses.

section_title: The Assembly
summary: The apostles and elders gather formally to consider the question of what is required of Gentile believers.

section_title: Peter's Speech -- God Already Settled This
summary: Peter testifies that God chose him to bring the gospel to Gentiles, gave them the Holy Spirit just as to Jewish believers, made no distinction between Jew and Gentile, and cleansed their hearts by faith; he warns against 'putting God to the test' by imposing a yoke that neither their fathers nor they could bear, and concludes: 'We believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will.'
relevance: Peter's declaration that salvation is 'through the grace of the Lord Jesus' (v. 11), with grace as the universal basis (not Law-keeping), has implications for the permanence question. If salvation rests on grace rather than on human performance under the Law, this could support permanence: what depends on God's grace may be more secure than what depends on human compliance. Additionally, God's unilateral act of cleansing hearts 'by faith' (v. 9) and giving the Spirit without distinction (v. 8) emphasizes divine initiative. However, Peter does not directly address whether the grace-based standing can be forfeited; his argument is about the basis of salvation (grace vs. Law), not its duration.
key_phrases: we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will
God made no distinction between us and them
cleansed their hearts by faith
God who knows the heart bore witness to them

section_title: Barnabas and Paul's Testimony
summary: The assembly falls silent and listens as Barnabas and Paul report the signs and wonders God performed through them among the Gentiles.

section_title: James's Speech -- Scripture Confirms What God Has Done
summary: James declares that Peter's testimony agrees with the prophets, quoting Amos 9:11-12 (LXX) to show that God's rebuilding of David's fallen tent was always intended to include Gentiles who bear God's name -- a purpose 'known from of old.'

section_title: James's Judgment -- The Four Prohibitions
summary: James rules that Gentile believers should not be troubled beyond four prohibitions (things polluted by idols, sexual immorality, things strangled, and blood) -- requirements corresponding to the Torah's provisions for the sojourner in Israel (Leviticus 17-18), creating the conditions for table fellowship between Jewish and Gentile believers.

section_title: The Letter
summary: The apostles, elders, and whole church send a letter to Gentile believers in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia, disavowing the unauthorized teachers, commending Paul and Barnabas, and declaring that 'it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay on you no greater burden than these requirements' -- the four prohibitions restated.

section_title: The Letter's Reception in Antioch
summary: The letter is read in Antioch and received with joy and encouragement; Judas and Silas, identified as prophets, encourage and strengthen the brothers; they are sent off in peace, and Paul and Barnabas remain in Antioch teaching and preaching.

section_title: The Separation of Paul and Barnabas
summary: A sharp disagreement (paroxysmos) over John Mark separates Paul and Barnabas; Barnabas takes Mark to Cyprus while Paul chooses Silas and departs through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.

section_title: Timothy Joins the Mission and the Decrees Are Delivered
summary: Paul circumcises Timothy (a man of Jewish maternal lineage) for practical reasons, delivers the Jerusalem Council's decrees to the churches, and the churches are strengthened in the faith and increase in numbers daily.

section_title: The Spirit Redirects the Mission to Macedonia
summary: The Holy Spirit forbids Paul from speaking in Asia, and the Spirit of Jesus blocks entry into Bithynia; a vision of a Macedonian man appealing for help leads Paul and companions to conclude that God has called them to preach the gospel in Macedonia -- the 'we' narrative begins as the author joins the party at Troas.

section_title: Philippi and the Conversion of Lydia
summary: At a riverside gathering in Philippi, Lydia -- a God-fearing businesswoman from Thyatira -- hears Paul speak, and 'the Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said'; she and her household are baptized and she prevails upon the missionaries to stay at her house.
relevance: The phrase 'the Lord opened her heart' (ho kyrios dienoixen ten kardian) attributes Lydia's receptivity to divine initiative. The neutral reading notes that 'her hearing is made possible by the Lord's prior action of opening her heart' and that 'the divine action enables human response; it does not replace it.' If the Lord must open the heart for faith to occur, this raises the question of whether what God initiates by sovereign action might also be sustained by sovereign action. However, the text addresses only the initiation of faith, not its continuation or permanence.
key_phrases: the Lord opened her heart to pay attention
divine action enables human response

section_title: The Slave Girl with the Spirit of Python
summary: A slave girl with a spirit of divination follows the missionaries proclaiming them 'servants of the Most High God who proclaim the way of salvation' -- factually accurate words from a false source; Paul, greatly annoyed, commands the spirit to come out in Jesus's name.

section_title: Economic Loss, False Charges, and Imprisonment
summary: The slave girl's owners, their revenue destroyed, drag Paul and Silas before the magistrates on fabricated charges of promoting unlawful customs; they are beaten with rods and thrown into the inner prison with feet in stocks.

section_title: Prayer, Earthquake, and the Opened Prison
summary: At midnight Paul and Silas pray and sing hymns while prisoners listen; an earthquake opens all doors and unfastens all bonds; Paul prevents the jailer's suicide by calling out 'We are all here.'

section_title: The Jailer's Question and Household Conversion
summary: The jailer asks 'What must I do to be saved?'; Paul and Silas answer 'Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household'; the word of the Lord is spoken to the entire household, the jailer washes their wounds, he and his household are baptized immediately, and 'he rejoiced along with his entire household that he had believed in God.'
relevance: The soteriological formula 'Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved' (v. 31) presents salvation as a direct consequence of believing, with no additional conditions mentioned. The future passive 'you will be saved' (sothese) presents salvation as a certain outcome of belief. The promise extends to the household. The neutral reading notes that the perfect participle pepisteukos ('having believed') describes the jailer's faith as 'a completed action with ongoing effect -- he has believed and continues in that belief.' However, the passage does not address what happens if belief ceases; it presents the positive sequence (believe -> be saved) without discussing the negative possibility.
key_phrases: Believe in the Lord Jesus and you will be saved
you and your household
having believed -- a completed action with ongoing effect

section_title: Roman Citizenship and the Magistrates' Fear
summary: Paul reveals his Roman citizenship, demands a public acknowledgment of wrongdoing from the magistrates who beat them illegally, receives their personal apology and escort, and visits Lydia's house to encourage the brothers before departing.

section_title: Thessalonica -- Reasoning from the Scriptures in the Synagogue
summary: Paul enters the Thessalonian synagogue and for three Sabbaths reasons from the scriptures, explaining and proving that the Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead and that 'this Jesus whom I proclaim to you is the Christ'; some Jews, many God-fearing Greeks, and leading women are persuaded and join Paul and Silas.

section_title: Jewish Opposition and the Charge of Another King
summary: Jealous Jews form a mob, attack Jason's house, and drag Jason before the politarchs with the charge that the missionaries 'are all acting against the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus' -- translating the messianic proclamation into the language of Roman treason; the politarchs take security bonds from Jason.

section_title: Berea -- The Nobility of Examining the Scriptures
summary: The Berean synagogue members are praised as 'more noble' because 'they received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so'; many believe, including prominent Greek women and men, until Thessalonian Jews arrive and stir up the crowds, forcing Paul's departure to Athens.

section_title: Athens -- Provoked by Idols, Reasoning in Every Setting
summary: Paul's spirit is provoked by Athens's idols; he reasons in the synagogue with Jews and God-fearers, and daily in the marketplace with passersby; Epicurean and Stoic philosophers dismiss him as a 'babbler' or a 'preacher of foreign divinities' and bring him to the Areopagus to explain his teaching.

section_title: The Areopagus Speech -- From the Unknown God to the Risen Judge
summary: Paul argues from creation and the Athenians' own religious practice -- the altar 'To the unknown God' -- through God's self-sufficiency, the unity of the human race, the inadequacy of idols, and the call to universal repentance, concluding that God has fixed a day of judgment through a man he appointed, whose authority is certified by his resurrection from the dead.

section_title: The Divided Response
summary: The audience divides at the point of the resurrection: some mock, some defer ('We will hear you again about this'), and some believe -- including Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris -- producing the smallest response of any city in Paul's journey.

section_title: Arrival in Corinth, Aquila and Priscilla, Tentmaking
summary: Paul arrives in Corinth, meets Aquila and Priscilla (Jews expelled from Rome by Claudius's edict, likely already believers), works with them as a tentmaker, and reasons in the synagogue every Sabbath trying to persuade Jews and Greeks.

section_title: The Arrival of Silas and Timothy, the Turn to Gentiles, Crispus
summary: When Silas and Timothy arrive from Macedonia, Paul intensifies his testimony that the Christ is Jesus; when the synagogue opposes and reviles him, he declares 'Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent. From now on I will go to the Gentiles'; he moves next door to the house of God-fearer Titius Justus, and Crispus the synagogue ruler believes with his entire household, followed by many Corinthians.

section_title: The Lord's Vision and Paul's Extended Stay
summary: The Lord speaks to Paul in a night vision: 'Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many people in this city'; Paul stays eighteen months teaching the word of God.
relevance: The Lord's declaration 'I have many people (laos) in this city' uses the covenant term laos -- the LXX word for Israel as God's chosen people -- to describe an uncollected, as-yet-unbelieving population in a pagan city. The neutral reading observes: 'God has a people in Corinth who are already his, who belong to him, who will respond when the word is spoken. They exist before Paul's preaching gathers them. They are God's prior possession -- a people who need to be found, not created.' This language of divine prior possession has implications for permanence: if God possesses a people before they believe, and their believing corresponds to God's prior claim on them, then their standing may rest on something more durable than their own decision. However, the text does not address what happens after they believe -- whether God's prior claim also guarantees their perseverance.
key_phrases: I have many people in this city
laos -- God's covenant people
God's prior possession
a people who need to be found, not created

section_title: The Gallio Incident
summary: When the Jews bring Paul before the proconsul Gallio on charges of promoting worship 'contrary to the law,' Gallio dismisses the case as an internal Jewish dispute about 'words and names and your own law,' establishing the first Roman judicial precedent that the Christian proclamation is not a violation of Roman law.

section_title: Departure from Corinth, Ephesus Visit, Return to Antioch
summary: Paul departs Corinth with Priscilla and Aquila, keeps a Nazirite vow at Cenchreae, briefly visits the Ephesian synagogue (leaving Priscilla and Aquila there), travels to Caesarea and Jerusalem, returns to Antioch, and departs on a third journey through Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples.

section_title: Apollos in Ephesus and Corinth
summary: Apollos, an eloquent Alexandrian Jew competent in the scriptures, arrives in Ephesus teaching accurately about Jesus but knowing only John's baptism; Priscilla and Aquila privately instruct him 'more accurately'; he crosses to Corinth where 'he greatly helped those who through grace had believed, for he powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus.'

section_title: Disciples Who Knew Only John's Baptism
summary: Paul finds about twelve disciples in Ephesus who had received John's baptism but had never heard that the Holy Spirit had been given; Paul explains that John's baptism was preparatory, pointing to 'the one who was to come after him, that is, Jesus'; they are baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus, Paul lays hands on them, and the Spirit comes with tongues and prophecy -- a small-scale Pentecost completing their incomplete faith.

section_title: The Synagogue, the Hall of Tyrannus, and the Spread of the Word
summary: Paul reasons in the Ephesian synagogue for three months about the kingdom of God; when some become stubborn (esklerynonto) and continue in unbelief, speaking evil of the Way before the congregation, Paul withdraws and separates the disciples, reasoning daily in the hall of Tyrannus for two years, so that 'all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks.'

section_title: Extraordinary Acts of Power
summary: God performs extraordinary miracles through Paul, such that even handkerchiefs and aprons that had touched his skin are carried to the sick, and diseases and evil spirits depart -- God is the acting subject, Paul the instrument.

section_title: The Sons of Sceva and the Failure of Borrowed Authority
summary: Itinerant Jewish exorcists, including seven sons of a high priest named Sceva, attempt to use 'the Jesus whom Paul proclaims' as a magical formula; the evil spirit responds 'Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you?' and the demonized man overpowers all seven; fear falls on the city and 'the name of the Lord Jesus was extolled.'

section_title: Confession, Renunciation, and the Burning of the Magic Books
summary: Existing believers (pepisteukoton -- perfect participle: 'those who had believed') come forward confessing and divulging their ongoing involvement in magical practices; those who had practiced magic arts burn their books publicly at a cost of fifty thousand pieces of silver; 'the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily.'
relevance: The passage reveals that believers had retained magical practices incompatible with their confession of Jesus as Lord. The neutral reading states that 'these believers had come to faith in Jesus but had not fully renounced the magical practices that pervaded Ephesian culture' and that the Sceva incident 'confronted these believers with the incompatibility between their faith in Jesus and their continuing reliance on magical techniques. They could not confess Jesus as Lord and continue to practice the arts that treated his name as one more incantation among many.' The narrative treats exclusive allegiance as a demand of the faith, not an automatic consequence of it. The fact that believers had to be confronted -- by the dramatic exposure of what happens when Jesus's name is treated as mere formula -- before renouncing their practices implies that ongoing transformation and exclusive commitment are expected but not guaranteed. The costly, irrevocable, public nature of the book-burning (destroying assets worth 137 years of daily labor) underscores that faithfulness requires active, costly choices after initial belief. However, the text does not explicitly state what would have happened had these believers failed to renounce -- it narrates the positive outcome without threatening a negative consequence for refusal.
key_phrases: those who were now believers came, confessing and divulging their practices
they could not confess Jesus as Lord and continue to practice magic
burned them in the sight of all
exclusive allegiance as a demand of the faith, not an automatic consequence

section_title: Paul's Resolve to Go to Jerusalem and Rome
summary: Paul resolves in the Spirit to pass through Macedonia and Achaia, go to Jerusalem, and then to Rome ('I must also see Rome' -- the dei of divine necessity); he sends Timothy and Erastus ahead to Macedonia while he remains in Asia.

section_title: Demetrius and the Economic Threat of the Gospel
summary: Demetrius the silversmith, whose guild manufactures silver shrines of Artemis, gathers the craftsmen and warns them that Paul's message ('gods made with hands are not gods') threatens their trade, the temple of Artemis, and the goddess's magnificence -- his argument begins with revenue, adds religion, and crowns it with civic pride.

section_title: The Riot
summary: The craftsmen incite a city-wide riot; the crowd rushes to the 25,000-seat theater dragging Paul's companions Gaius and Aristarchus; Paul is prevented from entering by the disciples and by friendly Asiarchs; Alexander, put forward by the Jews to distinguish them from the Christians, is shouted down when the crowd recognizes he is Jewish; the mob chants 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians' for two hours.

section_title: The Town Clerk Restores Order
summary: The town clerk quiets the crowd by affirming Ephesus's status as neokoros (temple keeper) of Artemis, declaring that Paul's companions are 'neither sacrilegious nor blasphemers of our goddess,' directing Demetrius to pursue legal channels, warning that the riot endangers the city's self-governing privileges with Rome, and dismissing the assembly.

section_title: Paul's Journey Through Macedonia, Greece, and Back to Troas
summary: The neutral reading describes Paul's travel itinerary from Ephesus through Macedonia to Greece and back, including the Jewish plot that forced a change of route and the list of traveling companions representing the collection-bearing churches.

section_title: The Gathering at Troas, Eutychus
summary: The neutral reading describes the community gathering on the first day of the week to break bread, Paul's extended discourse, Eutychus's fatal fall from the third-story window, and Paul's restoration of the young man to life in the manner of Elijah and Elisha.

section_title: The Coastal Voyage from Troas to Miletus
summary: The neutral reading narrates Paul's solitary walk to Assos and the coastal voyage south to Miletus, bypassing Ephesus because Paul was hastening to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost.

section_title: Paul's Address to the Ephesian Elders -- Review of His Ministry
summary: The neutral reading presents Paul's review of his Ephesian ministry, describing his service with humility and tears, his comprehensive teaching in public and from house to house, and his proclamation of repentance toward God and faith in the Lord Jesus Christ to both Jews and Greeks.

section_title: Paul's Resolve to Go to Jerusalem
summary: The neutral reading describes Paul as constrained by the Spirit to go to Jerusalem despite the Holy Spirit's testimony in every city that imprisonment and afflictions await him, declaring that he does not account his life of any value if only he may finish his course and testify to the gospel of the grace of God.

section_title: Paul's Declaration That They Will See His Face No More
summary: The neutral reading presents Paul's absolute declaration that none of his hearers will see his face again, his claim to be innocent of the blood of all based on the Ezekiel watchman tradition, and his assertion that he did not shrink from declaring the whole counsel of God.

section_title: The Warning About Wolves and False Teachers
summary: The neutral reading presents Paul's warning that after his departure fierce wolves will come in from outside the community and men from among the elders themselves will speak twisted things to draw away the disciples after them, requiring the elders to be vigilant shepherds of the flock the Holy Spirit has entrusted to them.
relevance: The warning that false teachers will arise to 'draw away the disciples after them' (apospao, 'to drag away, to pull apart') implies that believers can be separated from their proper allegiance to the Lord. The disciples are described as vulnerable to being pulled from their connection to the truth and drawn after self-serving teachers. The command to the elders to 'be alert' (gregoreo, the word Jesus used in Gethsemane) implies that ongoing vigilance is necessary to protect believers from threats to their faith, and that failure of vigilance has real consequences for the flock.
key_phrases: fierce wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock
from among your own selves will arise men speaking twisted things
to draw away the disciples after them
be alert

section_title: Commendation to God and the Word of His Grace
summary: The neutral reading describes Paul's commendation of the community to God and to the word of his grace, declaring that this word is able to build them up and to give them the inheritance among all those who are sanctified, followed by Paul's testimony of economic self-sufficiency and generosity.
relevance: Paul commends the community not to human leadership or institutional structures but to God and to the word of his grace. The word of grace is described as having inherent power (dynamis) to accomplish two things: to build the community up and to give them the inheritance among the sanctified. The emphasis on the word's capacity to secure the believers' inheritance suggests that the community's ultimate security rests in divine provision rather than human performance. The resource that sustains the community and guarantees its inheritance is God himself and his word, not the community's own effort.
key_phrases: I commend you to God and to the word of his grace
which is able to build you up
to give you the inheritance among all those who are sanctified

section_title: The Farewell
summary: The neutral reading describes the emotional farewell scene at Miletus: Paul kneeling in prayer with the elders, the community weeping and embracing Paul, grieving most of all because of his declaration that they would not see his face again, and escorting him to the ship.

section_title: Voyage to Tyre and the First Warning
summary: The neutral reading describes the sea voyage from Miletus to Tyre, where disciples told Paul through the Spirit not to go to Jerusalem, followed by a communal farewell prayer on the beach.

section_title: Caesarea, Philip, Agabus, and the Intensifying Warning
summary: The neutral reading narrates Paul's stay with Philip the evangelist in Caesarea, the prophetic sign-act of Agabus binding himself with Paul's belt to symbolize Paul's arrest in Jerusalem, and the community's unsuccessful attempt to dissuade Paul, ending with their acceptance of the Lord's will.

section_title: Journey Up to Jerusalem
summary: The neutral reading briefly describes the party's departure from Caesarea for Jerusalem, accompanied by early disciples who provide lodging with Mnason of Cyprus.

section_title: Meeting with James and the Elders, the Torah Question and the Vow
summary: The neutral reading describes Paul's warm reception by James and the elders, their report of zealous Torah-observant Jewish believers, the proposal for Paul to demonstrate his own Torah observance by sponsoring four men completing a Nazirite vow, and Paul's compliance with the arrangement.

section_title: The Temple Riot and the False Accusation
summary: The neutral reading describes the riot incited by Asian Jews who falsely accused Paul of bringing a Gentile into the temple, leading to Paul being dragged from the temple and the gates being shut.

section_title: Roman Intervention
summary: The neutral reading describes the Roman tribune's intervention to rescue Paul from the mob, Paul's arrest and binding with two chains, and the crowd's violence so severe that Paul had to be carried by soldiers up the barracks steps.

section_title: Paul Identifies Himself
summary: The neutral reading describes Paul's address to the tribune in Greek, dispelling the tribune's assumption that he was an Egyptian revolutionary, and Paul's identification as a citizen of Tarsus followed by his request to address the crowd in Hebrew.

section_title: Paul's Address to the Crowd in Hebrew
summary: The neutral reading describes Paul's opening address from the barracks steps in Hebrew (or Aramaic), producing a deeper silence from the crowd.

section_title: Paul's Jewish Credentials and Former Persecution
summary: The neutral reading presents Paul's recitation of his Jewish pedigree -- born in Tarsus, raised in Jerusalem, trained under Gamaliel, zealous for God -- and his former life as a persecutor of the Way, imprisoning and delivering men and women to death.

section_title: The Damascus Road Account
summary: The neutral reading presents Paul's account of his encounter with a great light from heaven near Damascus, the voice identifying itself as Jesus of Nazareth whom Paul was persecuting, and Paul's resulting blindness and helplessness.

section_title: Ananias and the Commission
summary: The neutral reading describes Ananias as a devout Torah-observant man who restored Paul's sight and delivered the commission: Paul is appointed to know God's will, see the Righteous One, hear his voice, and be a witness to all people, with the command to rise, be baptized, wash away sins, and call on the Lord's name.

section_title: The Temple Vision and Commission to the Gentiles
summary: The neutral reading describes Paul's vision in the Jerusalem temple where the Lord commanded him to leave Jerusalem quickly because the people would not accept his testimony, and the divine commission sending him far away to the Gentiles.

section_title: The Eruption at the Word 'Gentiles'
summary: The neutral reading notes the crowd's violent eruption the moment Paul spoke the word 'Gentiles,' revealing the precise theological boundary the audience would not cross.

section_title: Roman Citizenship and Its Legal Implications
summary: The neutral reading describes the tribune's order to examine Paul by flogging, Paul's revelation of his Roman citizenship before the flogging began, and the reversal of power dynamics as the tribune becomes afraid upon learning Paul is a citizen by birth.

section_title: The Tribune's Next Step
summary: The neutral reading describes the tribune's decision to bring Paul before the Sanhedrin to determine the actual nature of the accusation against him.

section_title: Paul's Opening Claim and the High Priest's Response
summary: The neutral reading describes Paul's opening claim of a clear conscience before God and the high priest Ananias's order to strike him on the mouth.

section_title: Paul's Rebuke
summary: The neutral reading presents Paul's sharp response to the high priest, calling him a whitewashed wall and accusing him of judging according to the Law while himself violating it.

section_title: Paul and the Office of High Priest
summary: The neutral reading describes Paul's acknowledgment that he did not know the man was the high priest, citing the Torah prohibition against speaking evil of a ruler of the people.

section_title: The Resurrection Divide
summary: The neutral reading describes Paul's strategic declaration that he is on trial concerning the hope and resurrection of the dead, which divided the Sanhedrin between Pharisees and Sadducees and effectively shifted the dispute from Paul's specific case to an intra-Jewish theological debate.

section_title: The Tribune Intervenes Again
summary: The neutral reading describes the tribune's intervention to extract Paul from the Sanhedrin by force as the dispute became violent.

section_title: The Lord's Appearance to Paul
summary: The neutral reading describes the Lord standing by Paul in the night and declaring that just as Paul has testified about Jesus in Jerusalem, so he must also testify in Rome, providing divine assurance of Paul's mission and survival.

section_title: The Conspiracy
summary: The neutral reading describes the oath-bound conspiracy of more than forty men who vowed neither to eat nor drink until they had killed Paul, with the cooperation of the chief priests and elders.

section_title: The Nephew's Discovery and Report
summary: The neutral reading describes how Paul's nephew learned of the conspiracy, reported it to Paul, and then to the tribune, who instructed the young man to tell no one.

section_title: The Military Escort
summary: The neutral reading describes the tribune's deployment of a massive military escort -- two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen, and two hundred spearmen -- to transfer Paul to Governor Felix in Caesarea.

section_title: The Tribune's Letter
summary: The neutral reading presents the tribune Claudius Lysias's letter to Felix, which describes the circumstances of Paul's arrest, his Roman citizenship, the religious nature of the charges, and the assassination plot.

section_title: Transfer to Caesarea
summary: The neutral reading describes Paul's transfer to Caesarea under military escort, his presentation to Felix, and Felix's decision to hear the case when the accusers arrive, with Paul held in Herod's praetorium.

section_title: The Prosecution Arrives
summary: The neutral reading describes the arrival of the high priest Ananias with elders and the orator Tertullus to present their case against Paul before Felix.

section_title: The Charges Against Paul
summary: The neutral reading presents the three charges against Paul: he is a plague and agitator among Jews throughout the empire, a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes, and he attempted to profane the temple.

section_title: The Prosecution Rests
summary: The neutral reading notes that Tertullus invites Felix to examine Paul and that the Jewish delegation joins in affirming the charges.

section_title: Paul's Defense -- The Facts
summary: The neutral reading presents Paul's factual defense: he has been in Jerusalem only twelve days, was not found disputing or stirring up a crowd in the temple or synagogues, and his accusers cannot prove any of their charges.

section_title: Paul's Confession -- The Way, the Law, and the Resurrection
summary: The neutral reading presents Paul's confession that he worships God according to the Way, believes everything in the Law and Prophets, and shares the same hope as his accusers in a coming resurrection of both the just and the unjust, which leads him to discipline himself to maintain a clear conscience toward both God and man.
relevance: The resurrection of both the just and the unjust establishes a universal judgment that distinguishes between these two categories -- a distinction that implies final standing is not automatically guaranteed. Paul's response to this belief is ongoing moral discipline: he 'always takes pains' (askeo, the language of athletic training and disciplined effort) to maintain a clear conscience. The logical connection Paul draws -- because there will be a resurrection of both just and unjust, therefore I discipline myself -- implies that the outcome of the resurrection is connected to one's conduct, and that even the apostle Paul does not treat his own standing as automatically secure but works to maintain it.
key_phrases: a resurrection of both the just and the unjust
I always take pains to have a clear conscience toward both God and man

section_title: What Actually Happened in the Temple
summary: The neutral reading presents Paul's account of what he was actually doing in Jerusalem: bringing alms and offerings to his nation, completing purification rites in the temple, without crowd or tumult.

section_title: Felix's Adjournment
summary: The neutral reading describes Felix's adjournment of the proceedings, noted as having a rather accurate knowledge of the Way, with Paul kept in custody but given some liberty.

section_title: Felix, Drusilla, and the Private Conversations
summary: The neutral reading describes Felix's private sessions with Paul in the presence of his Jewish wife Drusilla, where Paul reasoned about righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment, causing Felix to become alarmed, and Felix's hope for a bribe from Paul.

section_title: The Two-Year Imprisonment
summary: The neutral reading notes Felix's replacement by Porcius Festus after two years, with Paul left in prison as a political favor to the Jewish leadership.

section_title: The New Governor and the Renewed Conspiracy
summary: The neutral reading describes Festus's arrival as governor, the Jewish leaders' renewed request to transfer Paul to Jerusalem concealing an ambush plan, and Festus's counter-proposal that they come down to Caesarea.

section_title: The Trial Before Festus
summary: The neutral reading describes the hearing before Festus where the Jewish leaders brought many serious but unproven charges, and Paul denied any offense against the Jewish law, the temple, or Caesar.

section_title: The Favor, the Refusal, and the Appeal to Caesar
summary: The neutral reading describes Festus's attempt to do the Jewish leaders a favor by proposing a Jerusalem trial, Paul's recognition of the political maneuver and his refusal to be handed over, and Paul's formal appeal to Caesar as a Roman citizen -- a legal act that Festus must honor.

section_title: Festus Presents the Case to Agrippa
summary: The neutral reading describes Festus's presentation of Paul's case to King Agrippa and Bernice, noting Festus's characterization of the dispute as concerning the Jewish religion and a dead man named Jesus whom Paul claimed to be alive.

section_title: The Formal Hearing and Festus's Dilemma
summary: The neutral reading describes the formal hearing before Agrippa and Bernice with great pomp, Festus's statement that he has found nothing deserving death in Paul but needs help formulating the charges to send with the appeal to the emperor.

section_title: Permission to Speak
summary: The neutral reading describes Agrippa's invitation to Paul to speak in his own defense and Paul's expression of satisfaction at speaking before someone who knows Jewish customs and controversies.

section_title: Paul's Jewish Identity
summary: The neutral reading presents Paul's appeal to his well-known manner of life from youth in Jerusalem, his Pharisaic credentials representing the strictest party of the Jewish religion.

section_title: The Hope of Israel and the Resurrection Question
summary: The neutral reading describes Paul's framing of the trial as being about the hope of the promise made by God to the fathers -- the resurrection of the dead -- the same hope toward which the twelve tribes earnestly worship, asking why it should be thought incredible that God raises the dead.

section_title: Paul the Former Persecutor
summary: The neutral reading presents Paul's confession of his former opposition to the name of Jesus of Nazareth, including imprisoning saints, casting his vote against them when they were put to death, punishing them in synagogues, and pursuing them to foreign cities.

section_title: The Damascus Road Encounter
summary: The neutral reading describes Paul's third retelling of the Damascus road encounter: the light brighter than the sun, the voice speaking in Hebrew, and the self-identification as Jesus whom Paul is persecuting, including the proverb about kicking against the goads.

section_title: The Commission -- Content of Paul's Mission
summary: The neutral reading presents the content of Paul's commission: to be a servant and witness of what he has seen, appointed to open eyes so that people may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, receiving forgiveness of sins and an inheritance among those sanctified by faith in Jesus.

section_title: Paul's Obedience to the Heavenly Vision
summary: The neutral reading describes Paul's obedience to the heavenly vision, proclaiming to Jews and Gentiles that they should repent and turn to God, performing deeds consistent with repentance.
relevance: The content of Paul's proclamation connects genuine repentance to corresponding conduct: those who repent must 'perform deeds consistent with repentance' (axia tes metanoias erga prassontas). The adjective axia ('worthy of, befitting, corresponding to') establishes that repentance is not a one-time interior act but must be validated by ongoing conduct that corresponds to it. This echoes John the Baptist's demand in Luke 3:8 and implies that a repentance not accompanied by corresponding deeds is not genuine, creating a conditionality framework in which standing before God is tied to ongoing faithfulness expressed in conduct.
key_phrases: repent and turn to God
performing deeds consistent with repentance

section_title: The Message as Fulfillment of Moses and the Prophets
summary: The neutral reading presents Paul's claim that his entire message says nothing beyond what Moses and the prophets said would happen: that the Christ must suffer, be the first to rise from the dead, and proclaim light to both the Jewish people and the Gentiles.

section_title: Festus's Interruption
summary: The neutral reading describes Festus's loud interruption accusing Paul of madness from too much learning, and Paul's calm reply that he speaks sober truth that the king understands because these things were not done in a corner.

section_title: The Exchange with Agrippa
summary: The neutral reading describes the exchange where Paul appeals to Agrippa's belief in the prophets, Agrippa's response about being persuaded to become a Christian, and Paul's expressed wish that all who hear him would become as he is, except for his chains.

section_title: The Verdict of Innocence
summary: The neutral reading describes the private verdict of Agrippa, Bernice, and Festus that Paul has done nothing deserving death or imprisonment, and Agrippa's observation that Paul could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar.

section_title: The Decision to Sail for Italy
summary: The neutral reading describes the decision to send Paul and other prisoners to Italy under the centurion Julius of the Augustan Cohort, boarding a ship of Adramyttium.

section_title: The Coastal Voyage
summary: The neutral reading describes the voyage from Caesarea along the coast, Julius's kindness to Paul at Sidon, the difficult sailing past Cyprus due to contrary winds, and the arrival at Fair Havens in Crete.

section_title: The Debate About Continuing
summary: The neutral reading presents Paul's warning that the voyage would result in disaster and loss, the centurion's decision to follow the pilot and ship-owner rather than Paul, and the majority decision to try to reach Phoenix for wintering.

section_title: The Storm
summary: The neutral reading describes the sudden onset of the Northeaster wind, the progressive loss of control over the ship, the desperate measures taken, and the abandonment of all hope of survival.

section_title: Paul's Vision and the Angel's Message
summary: The neutral reading describes Paul's announcement that an angel of the God to whom he belongs and whom he serves appeared to him, declaring that God has granted Paul the lives of all who sail with him, and Paul's exhortation to take heart because he has faith in God that it will be exactly as he was told.

section_title: The Fourteenth Night and the Sailors' Escape Attempt
summary: The neutral reading describes the fourteenth night of the storm, the sailors' attempted escape in the ship's boat, and Paul's warning to the centurion that unless the sailors remain in the ship, the passengers cannot be saved.

section_title: Paul's Meal and the Breaking of Bread
summary: The neutral reading describes Paul's urging the 276 persons aboard to take food, his taking of bread with thanksgiving and breaking it before all, and the crew's subsequent lightening of the ship by throwing the wheat into the sea.

section_title: The Attempt to Beach the Ship
summary: The neutral reading describes the crew's attempt to run the ship aground on a beach, the ship striking a reef and running aground with the bow stuck fast while the stern was broken up by the surf.

section_title: The Soldiers' Plan and the Deliverance
summary: The neutral reading describes the soldiers' plan to kill the prisoners to prevent escape, the centurion's intervention to save Paul, and the complete deliverance of all 276 persons to land, fulfilling the angel's promise.

section_title: Malta, the Snake, and the Reversal of Judgment
summary: The neutral reading describes the landing on Malta, the islanders' hospitality, the viper that fastened on Paul's hand, the islanders' expectation that Paul would die as divine justice, and their reversal to calling him a god when he suffered no harm.

section_title: Healings on Malta
summary: The neutral reading describes Paul's healing of Publius's father through prayer and laying on of hands, followed by other islanders coming to be healed, and the community's generous provision for Paul's party at their departure.

section_title: The Journey to Rome
summary: The neutral reading describes the three-month stay on Malta, the voyage to Rome via Syracuse, Rhegium, and Puteoli, the welcome from brothers who came from Rome to meet Paul at the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns, and Paul's permission to live by himself with a soldier guarding him.

section_title: First Meeting with the Jewish Leaders in Rome
summary: The neutral reading describes Paul's first meeting with the Jewish leaders in Rome, his explanation of his situation, the leaders' response that they had received no negative letters about Paul from Judea, and their desire to hear his views since the sect is everywhere spoken against.

section_title: The Final Meeting, the Isaiah Quotation, and the Declaration to the Gentiles
summary: The neutral reading describes Paul's all-day exposition of the kingdom of God from the Law of Moses and the Prophets, the divided response of the Jewish audience, and Paul's final declaration citing Isaiah 6:9-10 about the people's self-imposed hardening, followed by the announcement that the salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles.
relevance: The Isaiah 6:9-10 quotation, presented in the LXX version, attributes the hardening to human agency rather than divine decree: 'their eyes they have closed' (ekammusan). The passage establishes a pattern in which relationship with God requires ongoing human responsiveness -- seeing, hearing, understanding, turning -- and in which humans can choose to close their eyes, stop their ears, and dull their hearts. The availability of healing is explicitly conditional: 'lest they should see... and turn, and I would heal them.' God is willing to heal, but the people must turn. While the immediate referent is Israel's initial response to the gospel, the principle that salvation requires ongoing human openness and that self-imposed hardening results in self-exclusion from God's healing has implications for the broader question of whether standing before God can be forfeited through human choice.
key_phrases: their eyes they have closed
lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn
and I would heal them
this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles

section_title: The Open Conclusion
summary: The neutral reading describes Paul's two-year stay in Rome in his own rented quarters, welcoming all who came to him, proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance.

section_title: The Greeting
summary: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy address the saints and faithful brothers in Christ at Colossae with grace and peace from God our Father.

section_title: Thanksgiving -- The Report of Their Faith
summary: Paul gives thanks for the Colossians' faith in Christ Jesus and love for all the saints, grounded in the hope laid up for them in heaven. The gospel has been bearing fruit and increasing since the day they heard and understood the grace of God in truth from Epaphras, their faithful minister. The section validates their original reception of the gospel and establishes Epaphras's reliability as a gospel messenger. Its primary concern is the authenticity of what they received, not the question of whether their standing is permanent or conditional.

section_title: Prayer for the Community and the Father's Rescue
summary: Paul prays for the Colossians to be filled with knowledge of God's will, to walk worthily, to bear fruit, to grow in knowledge, and to be strengthened for endurance. He gives thanks to the Father who qualified them for the inheritance of the saints in Light, rescued them from the domain of darkness, and transferred them to the kingdom of his beloved Son, in whom they have redemption and forgiveness of sins.
relevance: The section contains two movements. The prayer (vv.9-12a) seeks ongoing growth in knowledge, fruitfulness, and endurance, implying these require development. The rescue narrative (vv.12b-14) presents God's acts in completed terms: He qualified, rescued, transferred, and redeemed. The Exodus pattern is explicit -- as God delivered Israel from Egypt, so the Father has rescued the community from the domain of darkness and relocated them into the kingdom of his beloved Son. The completed verbs (qualified, rescued, transferred) describe accomplished changes of status that lean toward permanence. The redemption and forgiveness of sins are presented as present possessions ('in whom we have redemption'). The passage leans permanent because it attributes the community's new position entirely to God's initiative and completed action, though the prayer for ongoing growth and endurance in vv.9-12a qualifies the picture by indicating the community is not yet at its destination in terms of practical godliness.
key_phrases: qualified us to share in the inheritance of the saints in Light
rescued us from the domain of darkness
transferred us to the kingdom of His beloved Son
in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins

section_title: The Messiah's Relationship to Creation and Reconciliation
summary: The passage declares the Messiah's supremacy in two domains: creation (vv.15-17) and reconciliation (vv.18-20). He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation, the one in whom, through whom, and for whom all things were created. He is the head of the body, the church, the firstborn from the dead, the one in whom all the fullness was pleased to dwell, and through whom all things are reconciled by the blood of his cross. This is a Christological passage establishing who the Messiah is and what God has accomplished through him, rather than a direct argument about whether the believer's standing is permanent or conditional.

section_title: Application to the Colossians -- Reconciliation and Its Condition
summary: The cosmic reconciliation of vv.15-20 is applied personally to the Colossians. Though they were formerly alienated, hostile in mind, and engaged in evil deeds, God has now reconciled them in the Messiah's fleshly body through death, in order to present them holy, blameless, and beyond reproach before him -- if indeed they continue in the faith, firmly established and steadfast, and not moved away from the hope of the gospel.
relevance: This is one of the most directly relevant passages in the entire New Testament to the question of whether the believer's standing is permanent or conditional. The conditional particle 'eige' ('if indeed, provided that') introduces a genuine contingency into the argument. The neutral reading is emphatic: 'The conditional in this verse is not a throwaway formality. It introduces a genuine contingency into the passage's argument.' The reconciliation is real and accomplished (v.22a), the purpose is the community's presentation before God as holy, blameless, and beyond reproach (v.22b), but this presentation is explicitly conditioned on three ongoing postures: (1) continuing in the faith, (2) remaining firmly established and steadfast, and (3) not being moved away from the hope of the gospel. The neutral reading concludes: 'The author does not treat the community's continuation as automatic or guaranteed. He treats it as a real responsibility that corresponds to a real danger.' The three descriptions of the required posture all use language that presupposes the possibility of failure: one can discontinue, become unsteady, and be shifted. The passage directly and forcefully states that the outcome of reconciliation (presentation before God) depends on ongoing faithfulness.
key_phrases: if indeed you continue in the faith
firmly established and steadfast
not moved away from the hope of the gospel
to present you before Him holy and blameless and beyond reproach

section_title: Paul's Ministry -- Suffering, Mystery, and Maturity
summary: Paul describes his apostolic ministry: he rejoices in his sufferings for the community's sake, filling up what is lacking in the Messiah's afflictions. He has been made a steward of God's word to disclose the mystery hidden from ages but now revealed -- Christ among/in the Gentiles, the hope of glory. He labors to present every person complete in Christ, striving according to divine power at work in him.

section_title: Paul's Struggle for Communities He Has Not Met
summary: Paul reveals the intensity of his personal struggle for the Colossians, the Laodiceans, and all who have not met him face to face. His goal is their encouragement, their unity in love, and their full assurance in knowing God's mystery -- Christ himself, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden. He warns that he states this so that no one will delude them with persuasive arguments, and commends their current good order and firmness of faith. The section's primary concern is establishing the sufficiency of the wisdom found in Christ and warning against deceptive rhetoric, rather than directly addressing whether the believer's standing is permanent or conditional.

section_title: The Foundational Command -- Continue as You Began
summary: Paul commands the Colossians: as they received Christ Jesus the Lord, so they must walk in him -- rooted, built up, established in the faith just as they were taught, abounding in thanksgiving.
relevance: The imperative 'walk in him' (en auto peripateite) treats ongoing faithfulness as a command to be obeyed, not as an automatic outcome of initial reception. The logic is direct: 'you received Christ Jesus as Lord; now live within the reality of that reception. Do not add to what you received; do not look elsewhere for what you need; walk in him.' The four participial descriptions (rooted, built up, established, abounding in thanksgiving) describe qualities that must be actively maintained. The neutral reading notes that 'rooted' (errizomenoi, perfect tense) indicates a past action with ongoing effects, while 'built up' (epoikodomoumenoi, present tense) indicates an ongoing process. The instruction 'just as you were taught' implies the possibility of departing from the original teaching. The passage leans conditional because the imperative framework treats continuation as a responsibility, and the entire context anticipates the danger of being shifted (1:23) or taken captive (2:8) from this position.
key_phrases: as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him
rooted and built up in him
established in the faith, just as you were taught
abounding in thanksgiving

section_title: Warning Against Philosophy and the Fullness in Christ
summary: Paul warns the Colossians to see to it that no one takes them captive through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition and the elemental spirits of the world rather than according to Christ. He grounds the warning in the declaration that in Christ all the fullness of deity dwells bodily, and that they have been filled (pepleromenoi) in him who is the head of all rule and authority.
relevance: The theological claim of this section -- that all the fullness of deity dwells in Christ bodily and that the Colossians are filled in him -- has significant implications for the permanence question. The periphrastic perfect 'you have been filled' (este pepleromenoi) emphasizes the present state resulting from a past action: they are right now in a condition of having been filled. The fullness that dwells in Christ overflows to those who are 'in him,' making them complete. The completeness is presented as a present reality, not a future hope. The passage leans permanent because it declares that the community already possesses, in Christ, everything that God's fullness provides. However, the warning frame (v.8) qualifies the picture: the very fact that Paul warns against being 'taken captive' from this position implies that the community's enjoyment of this completeness can be disrupted by those who operate 'according to the elemental spirits of the world rather than according to Christ.'
